meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

Priority.desc: Direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

watches.desc: Watches follow one thread of an item on its own once a trigger event makes it worth it: an information-operations watch (kind "info-ops": official messaging, state-media narratives and documented influence campaigns), a shadow-war watch (kind "shadow-war": sabotage, incursions, cyber and influence below the threshold of war, and the targeted side's responses) or an operation watch (kind "operation": one named military operation, its gains, the enemy's response and what it shows). Each carries a narrower daily feed, plus dated findings and an assessment researched from open sources at each review.

types.official statement: Government, foreign-ministry, military or party statement aimed at an audience (strategic communications).
types.state-media narrative: Framing pushed by state or party media, including English-language outlets aimed abroad.
types.covert information operation: Documented coordinated inauthentic behaviour, disinformation or cognitive-warfare activity, attributed by a credible reporter.
types.coercive signalling: Military, coast-guard or legal action whose purpose is the message it sends.
types.sanctions/lawfare: Sanctions, lists or legal framing used to pressure or delegitimise.
types.counter-messaging: The targeted side's official response or rebuttal.
types.domestic narrative: Narratives inside the targeted polity (parties, polls, viral claims).
types.debunked claim: A specific false claim identified by a fact-checker.
types.third-party assessment: Analysis by a think-tank, researcher or major outlet.
types.hybrid attack: Physical sabotage, arson, cable or pipeline damage, cyber attacks, GPS jamming, drone or airspace incursions and other deniable attacks below the threshold of war.
types.defensive response: The targeted side's practical countermeasures: arrests, expulsions, airspace closures, deployments, new laws and alliance consultations.
types.territorial change: Ground or settlements gained or lost, with who reports it and whether it is independently confirmed (geolocated footage, ISW).
types.official claim: A command's or ministry's claim of gains, enemy losses or prisoners that has not been independently confirmed.
types.counterattack: The opposing side's counterattacks, reinforcements or renewed assaults in the operation's sector.
types.tactic or capability: A tactic, weapon or enabler used in the operation (drones, electronic warfare, converted vehicles, shaping strikes).

items.whyNow: Russia's largest energy strike of the year on 3 Nov cut Kyiv's water for more than 24 hours at the start of the heating season, and a glide-bomb strike on an aid point in Komyshuvakha on 2 Nov killed at least 43, days before working-level trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 Nov. The week tests whether grid repair and air defence can hold into winter as ballistic interception fell to about 18% on 3 Nov.
changes: 5 Nov: Kyiv's water supply failed again across all districts after voltage fluctuations and the metro was briefly halted; the Komyshuvakha toll reached 43 dead with 33 missing; Poland's ABW detained six suspects accused of supplying Russia with military-grade materials (Kyiv Independent).

4 Nov: Russia launched 310 drones overnight at energy sites with over 20 hits reported, and a milblogger claimed first use of the new Filin cruise missile near Dubrovytsia (single source); ISW assessed Russian forces consolidated north-western Kostiantynivka; Zelensky held a 90-minute call with Witkoff and Kushner ahead of Abu Dhabi (ISW, Kyiv Independent).

3 Nov: Russia's largest energy strike this year, 289 drones, 17 ballistic and 59 cruise missiles, hit nine oblasts with only about 18% of ballistic missiles intercepted, cutting Kyiv's water for over 24 hours; a strike on a Kharkiv hospital injured 73; Ukraine hit the Yaroslavl refinery; working-level trilateral talks were set for 10–11 Nov in Abu Dhabi with Medinsky leading Russia's team (ISW, Kyiv Independent).

2 Nov: Russian glide bombs, including a FAB-3000, hit a school used as an aid point in Komyshuvakha and then a shelter with nine more bombs, killing at least 40 by 4 Nov; Russia's emergencies app sent fake nuclear warnings after a cyberattack, a day after Ukraine's alert app was hacked (Kyiv Independent, Al Jazeera, ISW).

1 Nov: The Oleshky ceasefire ended as planned with about 800 people evacuated and no violations reported, though Ukraine's General Staff said Russia used it to rotate and resupply; Ukraine struck the Kstovo refinery and a Samara oil tank farm, and ISW put Russia's October net territorial loss at 27 km² (ISW, Kyiv Independent).

31 Oct: Ukraine hit two Ufa refineries about 1,200 km from the border and the Kamensky solid-fuel plant, as Russian strikes on a Kyiv heat and power plant and Dnipropetrovsk substations cut power to about 280,000 households; ISW noted new US PAC-3 interceptors are reportedly not due until after 2030 (ISW).

timeline.text: Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

A daylight Russian jet-drone raid hit Kyiv's National Academy of Sciences and killed five people across Ukraine, Zelensky said Russia had begun additional mobilisation as Putin enlarged the armed forces by 15,500, and the 3rd Army Corps closed Vivaldi's third stage with 51 square kilometres, three settlements and over 250 prisoners taken using converted BTR-60s as kamikaze vehicles.

Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones at energy sites around Kyiv and Kharkiv, leaving 600,000 without power, as the 3rd Army Corps claimed a fourth Vivaldi stage of 101 square kilometres north of Lyman.

Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, setting fires at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and Ruchi depot and hitting a VK data centre about 850 km from the border, its deepest mass raid of the war.

A limited humanitarian ceasefire around occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast took effect for aid deliveries and evacuations, the first agreed local truce of the year, while Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles and 280 drones.
A Russian jet-powered drone struck a passenger train platform in Dnipro and killed at least 14 people, hours after Moscow's mayor said 613 Ukrainian drones had been launched at the capital overnight.
Russian glide bombs, including a FAB-3000, struck a school used as a humanitarian aid point in Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and then a nearby shelter, killing at least 40 people.
Russia's largest strike on Ukraine's energy system this year hit power plants and substations in nine regions and caused emergency power cuts and widespread water outages in Kyiv.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status holds. ISW assessed on 1 Nov that Russia lost a net 27 square kilometres in October, its second monthly net loss, and on 4 Nov that Zarichne north-east of Lyman is a contested grey zone, yet Russian small-group infiltration still consolidated positions in north-western Kostiantynivka that day, so concealed movement under observation keeps buying ground slowly. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising status is borne out but the gap is widening at the top end: jet-drone interception reached 73.4% on 31 Oct–1 Nov and Kyiv fielded EW against mesh-networked strike drones (3 Nov), yet only about 18% of ballistic and anti-ship missiles were intercepted on 3 Nov and new PAC-3 deliveries are reportedly years away.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the Established and Contested status hardens on both sides. Russia's 3 Nov strike left Kyiv without water for over 24 hours because pumping lacks backup power, a single point of failure repair crews could not bridge, while Ukraine resumed refinery strikes at Ufa (31 Oct), Kstovo (1 Nov) and Yaroslavl (3 Nov), testing how quickly Russian throughput recovers.

watches.title: Russia–Europe shadow-war watch
watches.trigger: Russian helicopter and drone incursions into Poland, Romania and Moldova, 23–24 Sep 2026
watches.question: Is Russia escalating a shadow war against Europe below the threshold of open war (sabotage and arson, cyber attacks, undersea cable and pipeline damage, GPS jamming, drone and airspace incursions, shadow-fleet activity, espionage, assassination plots and influence or disinformation operations), through which channels and against whom, and how are European governments and NATO responding?

findings.actor: Polish police, Border Guard, army and intelligence services
findings.tactic: Pre-emptive security operation on Kaliningrad border
findings.text: On 2 Nov 2026 Polish police launched a special operation with counter-terrorism units along the Kaliningrad border in Warmia-Masuria and Podlasie after military and allied intelligence warned of possible sabotage, possibly including armed groups crossing the border. On the night of 2-3 Nov border guards saw people with flashlights near Sępopol and authorities said they had prevented a Russian provocation, but no crossing was confirmed and Tusk said the intent could not be established, so whether the deployment deterred an attack is unproven.

findings.actor: NATO (Baltic Sentry naval and air presence)
findings.tactic: Persistent patrols over Baltic undersea infrastructure
findings.text: NATO Assistant Secretary General Christian Buck told the European Parliament defence committee on 3 Nov 2026 that only one undersea-infrastructure incident, limited in scope, has occurred in the Baltic since Baltic Sentry began in January 2025, the last in January 2026, and that Russia has shifted to other domains. On that account the anchor-dragging pattern of 2023-2025 has been suppressed, but the figures are NATO's own and Buck conceded NATO cannot block shadow-fleet ships in peacetime or operate in the Black Sea (single source).

findings.actor: Unidentified hackers (no attribution; Russia suspected by some officials)
findings.tactic: Remote takeover of supermarket refrigeration controllers
findings.text: Overnight into 2 Nov 2026 fridges and freezers ran hot at more than 100 shops in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia, with temperatures in some cases set to 50°C, after a similar mid-October attack on hundreds of French stores. Attackers used internet-exposed, often end-of-life controllers with weak passwords; Belgian prosecutors opened an investigation and the EU agriculture commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt food supply. No one has claimed it and no government has attributed it to Russia, so its place in the Russian campaign is unproven.

findings.actor: Romanian Air Force (MApN)
findings.tactic: Scrambling F-16s against drone incursion
findings.text: On the evening of 31 Oct 2026 two drones entered north-eastern Romania during Russian strikes on Ukraine; Romania scrambled four F-16s and an IAR-330 helicopter and warned residents of six counties. One drone left Romanian airspace and the other was last tracked on the Vaslui-Bacău border; neither was reported shot down, so detection and warning worked but interception again did not.

findings.actor: Swedish police (border police, Stockholm region)
findings.tactic: Boarding suspected drone-depot cargo ship
findings.text: Overnight into 31 Oct 2026 Swedish police boarded an 80-metre dry-cargo ship with a Russian crew off north-west Gotland; TV4 reported that its owner is investigated over suspected use of its ships as depots for Russian intelligence drones near drone alarms across Europe. Police described a routine border check and said the documents raised no remarks, so the boarding produced no detention or public evidence (single source for the drone-depot suspicion).

findings.actor: Unidentified sea-drone operators (Ambrey: likely Russian Murena-300S-derived USVs)
findings.tactic: Sea-drone strike on merchant ship in EEZ
findings.text: Around midday on 28 Oct 2026 three uncrewed surface vessels hit the Liberian-flagged container ship Contship Jet about 17-21 nautical miles off Cape Kaliakra inside Bulgaria's EEZ, bound for Constanta; all 18 crew were rescued to Varna but the ship sank. A French patrol aircraft warned of a possible drone attack, yet Bulgaria could not stop it; Ambrey assessed the USV as likely derived from Russia's Murena-300S, Moscow denied involvement and no state has formally attributed it.

findings.actor: Bulgarian, Romanian and Turkish defence ministers
findings.tactic: Trilateral Black Sea early-warning and intelligence sharing
findings.text: Meeting in Sofia on 28 Oct 2026 while the Contship Jet was being hit, the three littoral states agreed to expand intelligence sharing, maritime domain awareness and early warning, and Turkey said it would keep applying the Montreux Convention as is. No escorts, patrols or interception rules were announced and the joint statement named no perpetrator, so the measure is untested; it follows a 20 Oct NATO surveillance surge that did not prevent the 23 and 28 Oct sinkings.

findings.actor: Munich General Prosecutor's Office and Bavarian police
findings.tactic: Pre-emptive arrest of paid arson cell
findings.text: Munich prosecutors announced on 28 Oct 2026 that two Belarusian men, aged 39 and 50, had been in custody since early October on suspicion of preparing arson against railway and power-transmission infrastructure in the Nuremberg area for payment by a foreign state; Der Spiegel and Romanian intelligence link them to a Russia-coordinated network. The plot was stopped before any attack, the first interdiction of this network that came ahead of the act rather than after it; German prosecutors themselves have not named Russia.

findings.actor: Russia-coordinated sabotage network (per Romania's SRI); Polish CBŚP
findings.tactic: Proxy arson at Romanian defence-industry site
findings.text: Polish police reported on 28 Oct 2026 the arrest in Warsaw of Artem S., a 25-year-old Ukrainian wanted by Romania, suspected of choosing the target and financing the 14 Sep arson at the Carfil site in Brasov next to a state arms maker; Romania's SRI says the network of post-Soviet nationals living in the EU took orders from Russia to hit arms plants. The arson itself went ahead, but within six weeks the network's organiser and two other members were in custody in Poland and Germany, so this cell has been rolled up; Moscow called the accusations baseless.

findings.actor: Cyber Army of Russia Reborn (GRU-linked, per US) and Z-Pentest
findings.tactic: Hijacking poorly secured industrial control systems
findings.text: A Bloomberg investigation relayed by Meduza on 28 Oct 2026 documented Russia-linked hacktivists causing physical effects through weakly protected industrial controls, from a Danish village pumping station (December 2024, 450 homes cut off, pipes burst; password reportedly "1234") to a Catalan transformer-factory fire, stopped winery systems and a US meatpacking ammonia leak. The method is crude but works where operators skip basic security; the response so far is sanctions, rewards and a handful of prosecutions rather than prevention, and CISA warns the groups also exaggerate their results.

findings.actor: Unidentified drone (Romanian President Dan: Russia)
findings.tactic: Aerial drone strike sinking ship off Constanta
findings.text: On the morning of 23 Oct 2026 a drone set the Comoros-flagged Khoryv on fire about 13 nautical miles off Constanta, just outside Romanian territorial waters; the ship capsized, one of 13 crew died and three were missing. Nothing was intercepted three days after NATO's Black Sea surveillance surge; President Nicusor Dan and Ursula von der Leyen blamed Russia, and Romania says it is still awaiting additional protective measures.

findings.actor: Unidentified drone (ISW: likely Russian); Moldovan police
findings.tactic: Drone overflight crashing near homes
findings.text: ISW's 23 Oct 2026 assessment relayed a Moldovan police report that drone debris fell about 100 m from a residential building near Chistelnita, Telenesti district, deep inside Moldova, and judged it a likely Russian violation of Moldovan sovereignty. The drone was not intercepted; Moldova can detect but still cannot shoot down such incursions, so the overflight pattern continues unopposed.

assessment.text: From 23 Oct to 5 Nov 2026 Russia's cheap remote tools kept working while defenders improved detection more than interception. Drones sank the Khoryv off Constanta on 23 Oct and sea drones sank the Contship Jet off Bulgaria on 28 Oct despite NATO's surveillance surge; on 31 Oct Romania scrambled four F-16s against two drones but downed neither. Unsecured industrial controls remain an open door: on 2 Nov hackers overheated freezers in more than 100 shops across five countries, though no state has attributed it to Russia. Countermeasures are working where they act early or persistently: German and Polish arrests rolled up paid arson cells by 28 Oct, and NATO said on 3 Nov that Baltic Sentry has left only one cable incident since January 2025 (single source), suggesting anchor-dragging has been superseded by other channels. Poland's warning-driven border operation of 2-3 Nov and Sweden's 31 Oct Gotland boarding produced no confirmed plot, so pre-emption remains unproven.

The strike continues the corps' October hits on Buk-M3 loaders, thinning Russian air defence over its strike drones, but the claim rests on the corps' own footage and does not assert destruction (single source).

findings.text: ISW's 4 Nov 2026 assessment cited a Western Grouping-affiliated source denying Russian claims to control Zarichne, calling it a contested gray zone where Russian units are still struggling to gain a foothold. ISW recorded no confirmed Russian advance in the Lyman direction, and Ukraine's General Staff reported further assaults near Stavky, Dibrova and Zarichne repelled on 5 Nov.

findings.tactic: Russian fast-following of Vivaldi methods
findings.text: Mick Ryan argued on 3 Nov 2026 that Russia, already a fast follower that copied Ukraine's mobile anti-drone groups and unmanned-systems force model, will try to emulate Vivaldi's deception, shaping strikes on fuel and depots, radio beacons keeping drones flying under GPS jamming, bomber-delivered and breaching UGVs and limited mechanised manoeuvre. No Russian copy has yet been observed on the Lyman front, so the question is open.

findings.tactic: Attacks east of Lyman, Zarichne and Yampolivka
findings.text: ISW reported that Russian forces concentrated attacks east of Lyman and in the Zarichne and Yampolivka areas on 1-2 Nov 2026 and continued operations within and near Lyman on 2-3 Nov without advancing, while Ukrainian forces counterattacked south, northeast and southeast of Lyman. ISW counts about 7.4 Russian attacks a day in the Lyman direction in October, down from 8.4 in September.

findings.tactic: Robots lead, armour and infantry follow
findings.text: Euromaidan Press reported on 1 Nov 2026 that in Vivaldi the 125th Brigade advanced behind robotic systems with armour and infantry following, exploiting gaps in the overextended Russian 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies, after rebuilding its line battalions to a reported 95-100% manning. The article also says the corps declared the operation finished on 19 Oct while elements reportedly kept pushing across the Zherebets; the brigade's figures are its own (single source).

findings.actor: Russian forces southeast of Lyman
findings.tactic: Infiltration into western Dibrova
findings.text: ISW's 30 Oct 2026 assessment cited geolocated footage published on 29 Oct of Ukrainian forces striking a Russian position in western Dibrova, southeast of Lyman, which it assessed followed a Russian infiltration mission. As at Zelena Dolyna on 28 Oct, the infiltration was found and struck without any Russian advance.

findings.actor: Russian forces near Yampil (per a Kremlin-affiliated milblogger)
findings.tactic: Holding Zherebets crossings to bog down Ukrainians
findings.text: A Kremlin-affiliated milblogger claimed on 29 Oct 2026, relayed by ISW on 30 Oct, that Russian forces control key Zherebets crossings near Yampil and aim to hold them for logistics and to draw Ukrainian forces into protracted fighting in the riverside forests. ISW did not confirm the claim; it mirrors the unconfirmed Ukrainian crossing claims further north and suggests the river line is now the contested edge of the operation.

findings.actor: Russian forces north of Lyman
findings.tactic: Infiltration raid near Zelena Dolyna
findings.text: ISW's 28 Oct 2026 assessment reported that Russian forces had recently conducted an infiltration mission north of Lyman and that geolocated footage published on 28 Oct showed Ukrainian forces striking a Russian serviceman east of Zelena Dolyna afterwards. ISW recorded no Russian advance, so infiltration into ground Vivaldi retook in its fourth phase is being detected and killed rather than gaining ground.

findings.actor: Ukrainian forces along the Zherebets (per open-source mappers)
findings.tactic: Crossing the Zherebets onto the east bank
findings.text: Euromaidan Press reported on 28 Oct 2026 that AMK Mapping and Suriyak claimed on 26 Oct that Ukrainian troops had crossed the Zherebets at several points, Suriyak naming Makiivka, Novosadove and Terny as a bridgehead, while AMK said many assaults had been repelled with rising casualties. The crossings are unconfirmed (Clément Molin could not confirm any on 20 Oct, Suriyak's own map shows west-bank positions) and ISW has reported none, so the push beyond the river is a claim, not a confirmed gain (single source).

findings.actor: Russian 25th Combined Arms Army and Western Grouping elements
findings.tactic: Ground assaults northeast and southeast of Lyman
findings.text: ISW reported Russian offensive operations in the Lyman direction on 22-23 Oct and northeast and southeast of Lyman on 24-25 and 25-26 Oct 2026, without any advance; a milblogger's 23 Oct claim of an offensive from Yampil toward Ozerne and Dibrova was not confirmed. ISW says Moscow has not formally abandoned its Fortress Belt plan despite what it calls the plan's operational defeat by Vivaldi.

findings.actor: Russian 50th Varyag Unmanned Systems Brigade
findings.tactic: Drone units replacing withdrawn Rubikon operators
findings.text: ISW assessed on 26 Oct 2026 that Russia had redeployed additional unmanned-systems elements to stabilise the Lyman front, citing the Varyag brigade's 26 Oct claim that its FPV crews were striking Ukrainian forces there, after elite Rubikon operators were reportedly withdrawn following heavy losses. This corroborates Militarnyi's 22 Oct single-video report: Russia is substituting drone formations for failed infantry pressure, but no regained ground has resulted yet.

findings.actor: NC13 unit, 3rd Assault Brigade (3rd Army Corps)
findings.tactic: UGVs and FPVs ambushing pipe infiltration
findings.text: Censor.net reported on 26 Oct 2026 that NC13 soldiers used ground robots and FPV drones to stop a Russian assault group trying to approach through a pipe during Operation Vivaldi, saying the attackers emerged in large numbers and were hit at once. The result rests on the unit's own video and account and is not independently confirmed (single source).

assessment.text: Between 23 Oct and 5 Nov 2026 Vivaldi's gains held and Russian attempts to retake ground failed. ISW recorded Russian attacks around Lyman, Zarichne and Yampolivka on 1-3 Nov with no advance, and infiltrations at Zelena Dolyna (28 Oct) and Dibrova (29 Oct) were found and struck; on 4 Nov even a Russian source called Zarichne a contested gray zone. Ukrainian methods keep working: ground robots and FPVs stopped a pipe assault on 26 Oct, the 125th Brigade advanced behind robots with armour following (1 Nov, single source), and drone operators struck a Buk-M3 on 4 Nov (single source), thinning air defence over strike drones. Russia's adaptation is to replace failed infantry pressure and the withdrawn Rubikon operators with the Varyag drone brigade, and to hold Zherebets crossings near Yampil to draw Ukrainians into forest fighting (claim, 29 Oct). With the corps having declared the operation finished on 19 Oct, the east-bank push is unconfirmed, and Mick Ryan on 3 Nov expected Russia to copy Vivaldi's methods.

timeline.text: After Iranian strikes on vessels collapsed the June ceasefire, US Central Command resumed its naval blockade of Iranian ports and struck Iranian anti-shipping targets near Hormuz.

After US strikes on Iranian coastal radars killed 11 people and the IRGC fired anti-ship ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer, CENTCOM destroyed or disabled three Iranian tankers, the Downy, Stark 1 and Kylo.

Trump publicly rejected Iran's seven-day plan after the Wall Street Journal reported he expects to resume bombing after the November midterms, and the next day the IRGC claimed a second US underwater drone captured in the strait, which CENTCOM called 'clearly desperate'.

The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank after a projectile hit in the Strait of Hormuz the previous day, one of two ships lost within a day, as security data showed at least ten vessels attacked since 11 October.

The IRGC claimed seven tankers hit overnight in and near the Strait of Hormuz, which Trump called fake and no maritime agency confirmed, a day after the New York Times reported US and Israeli plans for a short, intensive strike campaign on Iran after the 3 November midterms.

Trump reportedly told Gulf allies to prepare for a brief, intense campaign on Iran after the US midterms, as the IRGC claimed three tankers hit mines on the southern route and UKMTO confirmed one tanker struck by a projectile.

On the eve of the US midterms, US forces carried out limited 'defensive' strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island after IRGC surface-to-air fire at US aircraft, which officials said was not a resumption of major combat.

Two days after a midterm rout that Trump partly blamed on the war, Iran reported three more tankers hit in Hormuz as sources said renewed US strikes were still likely and Qatari mediation continued without a breakthrough.

text: Long-range strike versus integrated air and missile defence (Established · Contested) is borne out only in limited form: the campaign reportedly planned for after 3 Nov had not started by 5 Nov, but US aircraft struck Qeshm on 2 Nov after IRGC surface-to-air fire, showing the air-defence duel continuing at small scale, and the WSJ says such unannounced strikes have run for weeks. Mojtaba Khamenei's 31 Oct order to widen the target bank keeps the question one of how Gulf defences would absorb retaliation. Maritime chokepoint disruption versus energy-route resilience (Established · Contested) is strongly borne out: UKMTO counted at least five incidents from 1 to 5 Nov, near October's record pace, attacks reached 72 nm off Ras al-Khafji on 1 Nov, and a Qatari LNG carrier was hit on 30 Oct despite Iranian-cleared passage, so a permission regime is not protecting shipping.

Deterrence versus proxy and deniable escalation (Rising · Contested) is borne out: Iran pairs disputed mine claims with projectile hits UKMTO confirms, the US labels its strikes 'defensive' to avoid crossing into renewed war, and on 5 Nov Tehran named states aiding an attack as targets. Adaptability stays High on all three topics.

timeline.text: The United States, Israel and Lebanon signed a US-brokered Trilateral Framework tying phased Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament and creating a trilateral military coordination group.
Israel detonated about 1,100 tonnes of explosives to destroy Hezbollah tunnels under Ali al-Taher ridge and declared its south Lebanon security zone complete.

Hezbollah launched an explosive drone at Israeli troops inside the security zone overnight without causing casualties, the Israeli air force struck drone and anti-tank launch sites across nine southern localities in response, and Qassem told a Nasrallah-anniversary crowd that resistance continues until full expulsion and that Israel must first liberate the south before any dialogue.

Hezbollah publicly claimed a half-tonne explosives shipment seized by Lebanese security forces at Dahr al-Baidar, saying it was meant for use against Israel, a day after Israel's defence minister threatened to seize Nabatieh if Hezbollah joins an Iranian attack.

Two days of US-hosted Lebanon–Israel military talks at CENTCOM headquarters in Tampa ended without a breakthrough, with Israel rejecting Lebanon's demand for third-party verification of its army's operations.

Reuters reported, citing Lebanese security sources, that Hezbollah had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to rearm, focusing on explosives and attack drones and on rebuilding command and control.

Lebanon's military prosecutor charged 13 people over the Dahr al-Baidar explosives shipment, including two Hezbollah security officials still at large, and referred the file to an investigating judge.

An Israeli drone strike in Qabrikha, outside the buffer zone, killed a paramedic of the Amal-linked Risala Scouts, the first such fatality in south Lebanon since September, as Lebanon's prime minister warned against joining another war.

text: On border-zone security versus rocket, drone and dispersed-launch threats, the Established and Contested status is borne out as a one-sided contest: no Hezbollah fire on troops was reported in the fortnight, yet on 4 Nov the IDF struck two men on a motorcycle in Qabrikha, outside its zone, for observing troops, showing a forward-defence rule that treats surveillance as a threat. On precision strike versus escalation control, restraint now rests on coercive diplomacy more than fire: Israel asked Beirut on 2 Nov to set up army checkpoints in Hezbollah areas (single source, Kan), Rubio reportedly warned of strikes on Dahiyeh if Hezbollah backs Iran, and Trump said on 4 Nov there is no immediate plan to strike Iran, which lowers the near-term trigger without removing it.

On ceasefire monitoring versus armed-group reconstitution, the trigger status is close to firing in the institutional sense: the state charged 13 over the explosives shipment on 30 Oct and added charges on 2 Nov, Salam and Aoun publicly claimed the war decision on 4–5 Nov, but UNIFIL confirmed on 5 Nov that it leaves at year-end with no successor agreed.

changes: 5 Nov: The ASEAN Observer Team visited the Chey Chomneas checkpoint area in Veal Veng, Pursat; Cambodia's defence ministry said Thai forces had laid barbed wire, placed 52 containers, raised two flagpoles, built roads and deepened trenches inside Cambodian territory and called for the Joint Boundary Commission to start demarcation (AKP; Cambodian account, no Thai reply found).

4 Nov: Wang Yi hosted Prak Sokhonn and Sihasak Phuangketkeow for tea in Beijing on the sidelines of the 11th Lancang-Mekong foreign ministers' meeting; Xinhua reported 'constructive exchanges' on confidence-building between the two but no agreement (Xinhua; China Daily).

3 Nov: During an ASEAN Observer Team visit to Boeung Trakuon in Banteay Meanchey, Cambodia's defence ministry said 7,873 people (1,869 families) still cannot return home more than ten months after the ceasefire and accused Thai forces of razor wire, trenches and new fortifications (Phnom Penh Post via ANN; AKP; sources differ on the visit day, 1–3 Nov).

2 Nov: Defence Minister Adul Boonthumjaroen, after inspecting Ta Muen Thom, said the dispute is unresolved, that defence-ministry talks are on hold in favour of the Regional Border Committee deputy-secretary or military level, and that Cambodian attempts to climb Hill 642 are met under rules of engagement starting with dialogue and warning shots (Nation Thailand).

31 Oct: PM Anutin said crossings will stay closed and ties will not return to normal 'until Thailand gets what we believe it deserves': settlement of land and maritime areas, an end to scam networks using the border, and restored trust (The Thaiger; Khaosod English).

timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.

Hun Manet said the United States had asked Thailand to stop escalatory actions and encroachment on Cambodian territory, and Thailand's foreign ministry denied it the same day, conditioning any boundary commission meeting on a border secure from landmines and transnational crime.

The Hague conciliation round closed with the first agreed confidence-building measures (a direct channel between the two navies among them, by Thailand's account), while the Commission noted earlier measures were unimplemented and set a third meeting in Kuala Lumpur for 24–27 November.

Cambodia's culture ministry demanded the return of artefacts Thailand removed from K'nar temple and called Thai activity at disputed border temples a fait accompli, as the Thai army rejected Cambodian charges that its barbed-wire barriers were redrawing the boundary by force.

Thailand's defence minister said the boundary dispute was unresolved, parked defence-ministry talks in favour of the Regional Border Committee, and said troops facing Cambodian soldiers climbing Hill 642 apply rules of engagement starting with dialogue and warning shots.

China's foreign minister Wang Yi hosted his Cambodian and Thai counterparts for tea in Beijing on the sidelines of the Lancang-Mekong foreign ministers' meeting, discussing confidence-building measures between the two neighbours.

The ASEAN Observer Team visited the Chey Chomneas checkpoint area in Pursat, where Cambodia's defence ministry said Thai forces had placed barbed wire and 52 containers, built flagpoles and deepened trenches inside Cambodian territory.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving status is only partly borne out: no aimed fire or mine casualty was reported from 23 Oct to 5 Nov, but Thai troops used warning shots to turn back Cambodian soldiers climbing toward Hill 642, and on 1 Nov the Second Army Region commander ordered more wire and heavy weapons there (Thai accounts). Restraint now rests on graduated rules of engagement, which the defence minister restated on 2 Nov, rather than on a settlement. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the trigger has not fired, yet observers are documenting consolidation they cannot reverse: Cambodia said on 3 Nov that 7,873 Boeung Trakuon residents remain displaced and on 5 Nov that observers saw 52 containers, wire, new flagpoles and deeper trenches at Chey Chomneas (Cambodian accounts, no Thai reply found).

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the Background monitor status holds while the venue shifts: Anutin tied reopening to land, maritime and scam demands on 31 Oct, Bangkok moved talks down to the border committee on 2 Nov, and China, not ASEAN, hosted both foreign ministers on 4 Nov. Adaptability stays Low.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger has now been partly met: the 30 Oct strike on an ELN camp in Apure was Venezuelan-executed but, according to US officials cited by the New York Times on 3 Nov, enabled by US intelligence and drones, and the status-of-forces talks reported the same day point to sustained presence by consent rather than coercion. On information operations versus political legitimacy, the Rising status is borne out: Rodríguez promised elections on 29 Oct without a date, Machado pressed for one, and Rubio's 2 Nov meeting with the new foreign minister tied legitimacy to prisoner releases. Adaptability stays Medium, but the partnered-strike model, in which a host force executes against US-built targeting, is the most transferable lesson so far, although who flew the drones remains unconfirmed.

Pakistani nuclear adviser Khalid Kidwai said Islamabad will review its deployments to restore the strategic balance after reports that India had put nuclear warheads to sea on a submarine.
India flight-tested the Pralay quasi-ballistic missile off Odisha in a user evaluation trial, and the Defence Ministry said its induction was now imminent.

text: On cross-border strike and counterstrike versus escalation management, the Established · Contested status is only half borne out: no cross-LoC fire or lethal incident was found after the 17 Oct Keran clash, so the contest has moved into capability, with the 26 Oct clearance of 335 more K-9 Vajra howitzers and the 5 Nov Pralay user trial, which the Defence Ministry said makes induction imminent. On counterterrorism versus interstate deterrence, the Established status holds but its attribution logic is widening: India's spokesman said on 28 Oct that its post-Pahalgam Pakistan policy is unchanged despite the SCO invitation, and on 1 Nov Pakistan's military spokesman cast India as the 'prime contractor' of the TTP, the BLA and the Afghan Taliban, so a mass-casualty attack inside Pakistan could now be framed as Indian aggression. The 30 Oct FATF plenary added no jurisdictions to its grey list (single source), denying India a non-military lever.

On air, missile and information operations versus nuclear-threshold ambiguity, the Contested status persists in signalling: Pralay adds a conventional short-range strike option below the nuclear threshold, and India's 3 Nov vote against regional arms control rejects any South Asian balance framework. Adaptability stays High for stand-off strike and attribution contests.

timeline.text: Min Aung Hlaing is inaugurated as president of Myanmar's quasi-civilian military government in Naypyitaw, and on 21 April offers armed groups peace talks with a 100-day deadline that the KNU, CNF and NUG reject.
The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.

A junta fighter jet drops two bombs on the main wholesale market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, at about noon, killing at least 33 people and wounding 36 by the Arakan Army's and a senior rescue official's count, the deadliest strike in Rakhine since the December 2025 hospital bombing, with no comment from the military.

Junta warships, artillery and aircraft begin a week of failed landing attempts on Ngapyi Island opposite the Shwe Min Gan naval base near Sittwe, and by 14 October the Arakan Army still holds the island and has taken outposts on the city's edge, by local accounts.

The Arakan Army reportedly struck three navy vessels, including a frigate, near the Kaladan river mouth by the Shwe Min Gan naval base off Sittwe, sinking two, by anonymous military and AA-side accounts.

Junta airstrikes on four Rakhine townships killed at least 12 people, including a newborn at a makeshift maternity clinic in Arakan Army-held Mrauk-U, a day after a strike on a school in Loikaw killed three students.

Regime forces retook Alel, one of three villages on Ngapyi Island opposite the Shwe Min Gan naval base, by an anonymous Arakan Army source, after a counteroffensive reinforced with 1,000 troops on 30 October.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status is borne out: aircraft remain the regime's longest reach, killing at least 12 in Rakhine, a newborn at a Mrauk-U maternity clinic among them, on 1 Nov and at least three students in Karen State on 3 Nov, yet the Sittwe counteroffensive needed 1,000 extra troops for Ponnagyun from 30 Oct and has regained only Alel village on Ngapyi Island, on 4 Nov (single source). Airpower punishes populations without converting into ground control, while Arakan Army gains still stop short of taking Sittwe. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is not contradicted but the last 14 days add little that is verifiable: the claimed sinking of two navy vessels on 26 Oct is unconfirmed and its method unstated.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is reinforced at the borders: Thailand suspended informal Mae Sot trade from 30 Oct and summoned Myanmar's attaché on 2 Nov after spillover, while Naypyitaw courted the NDAA in Mongla on 1 Nov and a US strategy reported on 4 Nov ties peace diplomacy to rare-earth access. Adaptability stays High.

status.summary: The week's most significant development was the Houthi ground advance in Lahij on 1–2 Nov that brought them to within about 80 km of Aden, alongside continued missile and drone fire at Saudi Arabia, including the Medina region on 5 Nov, and a Houthi missile strike on a recruit camp in al-Dhale on 4 Nov. Over the week the Saudi–Houthi war held at a daily tempo with most attacks on the kingdom intercepted, while the fight in Yemen widened on the ground, regional alignments deepened with Turkey's move to ratify a defence pact, and no corroborated attack on Red Sea shipping was reported.
